title: Ms. H & AirNav Ireland
text:
Decision
Ms. H & AirNav Ireland
From
Office of the Commissioner for Environmental Information (OCEI)
Case number: OCE-163101-Y7J7V5
Published on 16 June 2026
Context
Background
Scope of Review
Analysis and Findings
Decision
Appeal to the High Court
Whether the information requested by the appellant is “environmental information” within the meaning of the definition of article 3(1) of the AIE regulations.
16 June 2026
Context
R116 Air Accident
1. As detailed in the Air Accident Investigation Unit Report (‘AAIU’) final report, on March 14, 2017, a Sikorsky S-92A helicopter, registration EI-ICR (call sign Rescue 116), which was being operated by a private operator on behalf of the Irish Coast Guard, was en route from Dublin to Blacksod, Co. Mayo. It was the Flight Crew’s intention was to refuel at Blacksod before proceeding, as tasked, to provide Top Cover for another of the Operator’s helicopters, which had been tasked to airlift a casualty from a fishing vessel, situated approximately 140 nautical miles off the west coast of Ireland. At 00.46 hrs while positioning for an approach to Blacksod from the west, the Helicopter, which was flying at 200 feet above the sea, collided with terrain at the western end of Black Rock, departed from controlled flight, and impacted with the sea, resulting in the tragic loss of all four crew members. The appellant’s request for information under the AIE Regulations is related to this air accident.
The relevant Public Authority
2. The appellant made her original request to the Irish Aviation Authority (‘IAA’) on the 17 May 2022. As confirmed by AirNav Ireland, the air navigation services functions of the IAA moved to AirNav Ireland on 30 April 2023. Therefore, it is necessary to outline this restructuring within the IAA as it relates to the appellant’s AIE request.
3. On review of the IAA’s website, it is described as a commercial semi-state company and the single civil aviation regulator for Ireland. The IAA is responsible for the regulation of safety, security and consumer interests.
4. According to the IAA’s annual report 2024, the Air Navigation and Transport Act 2022 provided for the restructuring of Ireland’s civil aviation regulatory framework to ensure compliance with international best practice. The Act provided for the merger of the safety and security regulation functions of the IAA with the economic and consumer protection functions of the Commission for Aviation Regulation, within IAA, to create a single civil aviation regulator. It also provided for the air navigation functions of the IAA to transfer to a separate commercial, semi-state company, the Irish Air Navigation Service DAC trading as AirNav Ireland. This merger and separation formally took place on 01 May 2023.
5. As the appellant’s current appeal to this Office is post this restructure, her appeal is being processed by AirNav Ireland as the public authority now holding the relevant records.
Background
6. On 17 May 2022 the appellant made the following request to the IAA under the AIE Regulations:
a. “A copy of the report prepared by the Air Traffic Controllers on the R116 crash at Blacksod Bay in March 2017. I am requesting a copy of this report under the Access to Information on the environment regulations on the basis to see what role environmental factors such as weather conditions, geographic location, air traffic conditions etc., contributed to this accident.
b. I am also requesting all written correspondence including e-mails, faxes, letters, memos, text messages including those on social messaging apps such as Whatsapp, to do with this report and its findings under the same regulations.”
7. On 17 July 2022 the IAA responded by furnishing the appellant with a report and stated that the requested information was included in this report.
8. On 26 July 2022, the appellant requested an internal review. The appellant submitted that the report that issued was the final IAA report and not the Air Traffic Controller’s report as requested.
9. On 25 August 2022, the IAA replied to the appellant affirming the original decision on the basis that operational data is protected under regulation 376/2014. Regulation 376 of 2014 is a European Union Regulation concerning the reporting, analysis and follow up of occurrences in civil aviation. The IAA confirmed that the AAIU is the competent authority for the State and that it is the appropriate body from which any such information should be requested.
10. The appellant brought an appeal to this Office on 30 August 2022.
11. In the decision on that appeal
OCE-127739-F6N9X8
dated 30 November 2023, the Commissioner found that the request had not been dealt with in accordance with Articles 3(4) and 4(5) of the Directive, stated that the IAA must comply with the AIE Regulations and advised it to immediately put in place appropriate measures to ensure proper engagement with requesters and with this Office in relation to AIE appeals.
12. The Commissioner annulled the IAA’s decision and remitted the matter for fresh consideration by the IAA with the expectation that the fresh decision-making progress would culminate in a decision which complies with the requirements of the AIE Regulations and the AIE Directive.
13. Following this decision, a new internal review decision does not appear to have been issued to the appellant. As a result, the appellant was obliged to contact AirNav (post the restructure) on the 24 July 2025, requesting this new internal review, some twenty months later.
14. On the 15 September 2025, AirNav Ireland issued a new internal review decision to the appellant in which it identified two records falling within the scope of the appellant’s request, it confirmed that refusal to release these records was based on articles 8(a)(iv) and 9(1)(b) of the AIE regulations. I note there was a delay to the statutory timeframes here, this appears to have occurred around the same time that IAA underwent a significant restructure, as I have set out above.
15. The appellant brought an appeal to this Office on 01 October 2025. The appellant in her appeal sought a review of the internal review of 15 September 2025 on the following basis:
“AirNav are refusing to release information sought on the basis that to do so would:
1) Adversely affect confidentiality.
2) A High Court Order is required.
3) Would impact the course of justice and criminal inquiries.
4) The public interest of releasing is outweighed by the public interest of withholding.
However, there are no on-going criminal inquiries or investigations. The final report has been completed and its findings were published four years ago in November 2021. In addition, when this final report was released voice recordings of those on board were broadcasted on the national television even though a High Court order was neither sought nor granted.
The R116 crash is regarded as the worse aviation accident involving a search and rescue team in the country's history. Two bodies were recovered and the bodies of two others have yet to be recovered. So given all of the reasons cited above by me the public interest in releasing this information far outweighs the public interest of not doing so."
16. I am directed by the Commissioner for Environmental Information to carry out a review of this appeal. I have now completed this review under article 12(5) of the Regulations. In carrying out my review, I have had regard to the submissions made by the appellant and by the Department. In addition, I have had regard to:
• the Guidance document provided by the Minister for the Environment, Community and Local Government on the implementation of the AIE Regulations (the Minister’s Guidance);
• Directive 2003/4/EC (the AIE Directive), upon which the AIE Regulations are based;
• the 1998 United Nations Economic Commission for Europe Convention on Access to Information, Public Participation in Decision-Making and Access to Justice in Environmental Matters (the Aarhus Convention); and
• The Aarhus Convention—An Implementation Guide (Second edition, June 2014) (‘the Aarhus Guide’).
• The judgments of the Superior Courts in Redmond & Anor v Commissioner for Environmental Information & Anor [2020] IECA 83 (Redmond), Electricity Supply Board v Commissioner for Environmental Information & Lar Mc Kenna [2020] IEHC 190 (ESB) and Right to Know v Commissioner for Environmental Information & RTÉ [2021] IEHC 353 (RTÉ).
• The judgment of the Court of Appeal of England and Wales in Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy v Information Commissioner and Henney [2017] EWCA Civ 844 (Henney) which is referenced in the decisions in Redmond, ESB and RTÉ; and
• The decisions of the Court of Justice of the European Union in C-321/96 Wilhelm Mecklenburg v Kreis Pinneberg - Der Landrat (Mecklenburg), and C-316/01 Eva Glawischnig v Bundesminister für soziale Sicherheit und Generationen (Glawischnig).
• The judgment of the Court of Appeal in Electricity Supply Board -v- Commissioner for Environmental Information [2026] IECA 57.
17. What follows does not comment or make findings on each and every argument advanced, but all relevant points have been considered.
Scope of Review
18. In accordance with article 12(5) of the AIE Regulations, my role is to review the public authority’s internal review decision and to affirm, annul or vary it. Where appropriate in the circumstances of an appeal, I will require the public authority to make available environmental information to the appellant.
19. My powers as Commissioner for Environmental information apply only in respect of environmental information held by or for the public authority and the matter of whether the information sought is “environmental information” is a threshold jurisdictional question. I am cognisant that in my previous decision in respect of this request for information,
OCE-127739-F6N9X8
dated 30 November 2023, that the issue as to whether the information sought in the appellant’s request was environmental information pursuant to 3(1) of the AIE Regulations did not arise, and it was therefore not addressed in the decision.
20. A review by this Office is considered to be de novo, which means that it is based on the circumstances and the law as they pertain at the time of this decision. This approach has been endorsed by the decision of the High Court in M50 Skip Hire Recycling Limited v the Commissioner for Environmental Information 2020 IEHC 430. Further it is clear from the comments of the Court of Appeal in Redmond, at paragraph 51, that the nature of a review by this Office is inquisitorial, rather than adversarial in nature. The extent of the inquiry is determined by this Office, and not by the parties to the appeal.
21. In this regard, given the de novo nature of reviews conducted by this Office, I am satisfied that it appropriate in this appeal to focus on the matter of whether the information sought is “environmental information” such that it falls within the remit of article 3(1) of the AIE Regulations.
22. If it is determined that the subject information does fall within 3(1) then it will be necessary to address AirNav Ireland’s refusal to release the records based on articles 8(a)(iv) and 9(1)(b) of the AIE regulations. However, if it is determined that the information subject of the appeal is not considered to be environmental information in accordance with article 3(1) of the AIE Regulations then that is the end of the matter, as I only have the power to make an assessment of the application of articles 8(a)(iv) and 9(1)(b) of the AIE regulations by AirNav Ireland in respect of “environmental information.”
Analysis and Findings
Position of the parties
23. In a submission to this Office dated 30 April 2026, Air Nav stated the following in respect of article 3(1), “AirNav Ireland notes the provisions of Article 3(1) of the AIE Regulations and the associated case law. AirNav Ireland is of the view that the information sought under the request is not environmental information within the meaning of Article 3(1) of the AIE Regulations.”
24. In response to the investigators preliminary view and AirNav Ireland’s submission, the appellant in a submission dated 14 May 2026 stated, “I do not agree with that view, and I am asking that the Commissioner finds that the records requested; or at least parts of them; do fall within article 3(1) of the said Regulations.” The appellant’s arguments included but were not limited to the following points.
25. The appellant stated that her request relates to “a report prepared by Air Traffic Controllers into the R116 crash at Blacksod Bay in March 2017, along with all related written communications (including emails, messages, memos, etc.) about that report and its findings and it this is not just about a past aviation incident; it’s about how that incident was reviewed and discussed by air traffic control personnel”.
26. The appellant confirmed acceptance that “the key issue is whether the material qualifies as “environmental information” under article 3(1), and that there must be more than a minimal link to the environment. However, the case law also makes clear that the definition is broad, and information does not have to be purely environmental in nature to come within scope.”
27. The appellant submitted that the “real question is whether the content of the records fits within one or more of the categories in article 3(1), rather than how the records might be labelled in general terms. In my view, the records clearly have the potential to fall within article 3(1)(c), which covers information on measures or activities affecting, or likely to affect, environmental elements” and in her view “a report by Air Traffic Controllers into a helicopter crash, along with related communications, is capable of including information about air navigation, air traffic control, aviation safety, operational procedures, emergency response, and accident prevention. These are regulated public safety activities that operate within the air and atmosphere, and in this case relate directly to an incident at a coastal location”.
28. The appellant submitted that the information requested potentially falls under article 3(1)(a), (b), (c) and/or (f) as follows:
“If the report or correspondence deals with matters like routing, communications, weather, visibility, marine conditions, emergency response, or lessons learned, then those parts of the records are clearly about activities or measures within article 3(1)(c). Similarly, the records may fall within article 3(1)(f), which covers human health and safety where it is affected by environmental factors or related activities. The R116 crash involved loss of life in a coastal/marine environment. Any reasonable analysis of safety, conditions, or operational response is capable of engaging article 3(1)(f).
It would be too narrow to treat this provision as limited to pollution or public health scenarios only. Article 3(1)(a) is also relevant, as it includes environmental elements such as air, atmosphere, water, and coastal and marine areas. Given that the crash occurred at Blacksod Bay, any discussion of weather, visibility, terrain, or marine conditions would surely fall within this category.
Likewise, article 3(1)(b) may be engaged if the records refer to fuel, debris, emissions, noise, or any other releases, including human remains into the environment arising from the crash or recovery operations. Whether this applies will depend on the content, which is why a detailed assessment of the records is important. The broader aviation law context supports this approach.
Air traffic control and aviation safety functions are part of a regulated public safety system, and accident review processes are aimed at preventing future incidents. This reinforces the view that these are “measures or activities” within the meaning of article 3(1)(c). I am not suggesting that every aviation-related record is environmental information. But records relating to the review of a helicopter crash in a coastal setting are clearly capable of falling within scope, depending on what they contain.
In that context, AirNav Ireland’s position; as outlined in your letter; seems far too conclusory. It doesn’t explain, by reference to the actual contents of the records, nor why they would not fall within any part of article 3(1). A broad general assertion that they are not environmental information simply is not sufficient in circumstances like this.”
29. The appellant further submitted as her request “covers multiple records, not just a single document. Some parts may fall within the definition even if others do not. For this reason, I ask that the records are considered individually, or at least on a part-by-part basis, rather than as a single category.”
30. The appellant asked that “the Commissioner not to adopt the preliminary view that the requested information falls outside article 3(1). Instead, I ask that it be found that the records - or relevant parts of them - fall within article 3(1)(a), (b), (c) and/or (f), particularly as information relating to aviation safety, air navigation, operational review, and accident prevention. If that conclusion cannot be reached for all of the material, I request that the records be assessed in detail and that any parts falling within the definition be identified accordingly.”
31. Finally, the appellant stated that “RTÉ’s Prime Time special on the Rescue 116 crash, broadcast on 5 November 2021, the night before the AAIU final report was published, played actual transmissions between the helicopter and Dublin Air Traffic Control”.
Definition of Environmental Information
32. Article 3(1) of the AIE Regulations is the relevant provision to consider where the issue is whether information is "environmental information". In line with Article 2(1) of the AIE Directive, article 3(1) of the AIE Regulations provides that "environmental information" means:
“any information in written, visual, aural, electronic or any other material form on —
(a) the state of the elements of the environment, such as air and atmosphere, water, soil, land, landscape and natural sites including wetlands, coastal and marine areas, biological diversity and its components, including genetically modified organisms and the interaction among these elements,
(b) factors, such as substances, energy, noise, radiation or waste, including radioactive waste, emissions, discharges and other releases into the environment, affecting or likely to affect the elements of the environment
(c) measures (including administrative measures), such as policies, legislation, plans, programmes, environmental agreements, and activities affecting or likely to affect the elements and factors referred to in paragraphs (a) and (b) as well as measures or activities designed to protect those elements,
(d) reports on the implementation of environmental legislation,
(e) cost-benefit and other economic analyses and assumptions used within the framework of the measures and activities referred to in paragraph (c), and
(f) the state of human health and safety, including the contamination of the food chain, where relevant, conditions of human life, cultural sites and built structures inasmuch as they are, or may be, affected by the state of the elements of the environment referred to in paragraph (a) or, through those elements, by any of the matters referred to in paragraphs (b) and (c).”
33. The right of access under the AIE Regulations is to information “on” one or more of the six categories at (a)to (f) of the definition. According to national and EU case law on the definition of “environmental information”, while the concept of “environmental information as defined in the AIE Directive is broad (Mecklenburg at paragraph 19), there must be more than a minimal connection with the environment (Glawisching at paragraph 25). Information does not have to be intrinsically environmental to fall within the scope of the definition (Redmond at paragraph 58; see also ESB at paragraph 43). However, a mere connection of link to the environment is not sufficient to bring information within the definition of environmental information. Otherwise, the scope of the definition would be unlimited in a manner that would be contrary to the judgments of the Court of Appeal and the CJEU.
Identification of a measure or activity
34. Paragraph (c) requires the identification of a relevant measure or activity, which the information sought is “on”.
35. When identifying a measure, it is useful to draw on the relevant case law. Information may be “on” more than one measure or activity ( Henney
at paragraph 42). The Irish Court of Appeal in ESB (paragraph 76) referred to Henney
, where Beatson L.J. accepted that it was permissible to look beyond the precise issue with which the information is concerned (which in this case is the Air Traffic Controllers investigation report into the R116 air crash) to identify the measure, but not to look at issues with which the information is not concerned or with which it is merely connected (para. 39). He did not go so far as to require that the information be “directly or immediately concerned”
with the measure so as to exclude consideration of the broader context. He stated (at para. 43 of the judgment):
“It follows that identifying the measure that the disputed information ‘on’ may require consideration of the wider context, and is not strictly limited to the precise issue with which the information is concerned, here the communications and data component, or the document containing the information, here the Project Assessment Review. It may be relevant to consider the purpose for which the information was produced, how important the information is to that purpose, how it is to be used and whether access to it would enable the public to be informed about, or to participate in, decision-making in a better way. None of these matters may be apparent on the face of the information itself. It was not in dispute that, when identifying the measure, a tribunal should apply the definition in the [Regulations] purposively, bearing in mind the modern approach to the interpretation of legislation, and particularly to international and European measures such as the Aarhus Convention and the Directive. It is then necessary to consider whether the measure so identified has the requisite environmental impact for the purposes of regulation 2(1).”
36. The Irish Courts have made clear that when identifying the relevant measure or activity, one may consider the wider context and is not strictly limited to the precise issue with which the information is concerned (ESB No. 1 at paragraph 43). Further, the list of examples of measures and activities given at paragraph (c) is not exhaustive, but it contains illustrative examples (Redmond at paragraph 55). The Court of Justice of the European Union (‘CJEU’) stated in Mecklenburg that the term ‘measure’ serves “merely to make it clear that the acts governed by the directive included all forms of administrative activity” (Mecklenburg at paragraph 20), and the Irish Courts adopted a similarly expansive approach should be taken to the term ‘activity’ (RTÉ at paragraph 19).
37. In my opinion the most appropriate and relevant measure here in respect of the request is the Air Traffic Controllers investigation into the R116 air accident. This is the case in respect of both parts of the appellant’s AIE request, which are clearly interrelated.
38. The records subject to this review are identified by AirNav Ireland as the “Safety Management Unit's Report” and a “Partial transcript of Shannon Air Traffic Control to aircraft R116”. AirNav Ireland submitted by way of explanation that the Safety Management Unit's Report “constitutes opinion expressed in the analysis of information, including CVR and FDR information, by the safety management unit of the IAA when carrying out an investigation into the accident involving aircraft callsign R116” (CVR being Cockpit Voice recordings and FDR being Flight Deck Recordings) and that “Partial transcript of Shannon Air Traffic Control to aircraft R116” “constitutes a transcript of a recording from an air traffic control unit.”
39. Both records relate to the R116 air accident and are incident specific operational and communicative records, created for safety and operational purposes. I am of the view that the overarching measure to which both of these records relate is the Air Traffic Controllers investigation into the R116 air accident.
40. In my view, paragraph (c) of the definition of environmental information provided for in article 3(1) of the Regulations, which provides that environmental information” means any information on “measures (including administrative measures), such as policies, legislation, plans, programmes, environmental agreements, and activities affecting or likely to affect the elements and factors referred to in paragraphs (a) and (b) as well as measures or activities designed to protect those elements, is the only paragraph relevant to this review.
41. The next issue to be considered is whether the measure, in this case the Air Traffic Controllers investigation into the R116 air accident, affects or is likely to affect or designed to protect the environment.
Whether the measure or activity is affecting, likely to affect or designed to protect the environment
42. A measure or activity is “likely to affect” the elements and factors of the environment if there is a real and substantial possibility that it will affect the environment, whether directly or indirectly. Collins J, delivering judgment on behalf of the Court of Appeal in Redmond, noted that “63. Drawing together these statements, it appears to me that, for the purposes of paragraph (c), a measure or activity is “likely to affect” the environment if there is a real and substantial possibility that it will affect the environment, whether directly or indirectly. Something more than a remote or theoretical possibility is required (because that would sweep too widely and could result in the “general and unlimited right of access” that Glawischnig indicates the AIE Directive was not intended to provide) but it is not necessary to establish the probability of a relevant environmental impact (because that would, in my opinion, sweep too narrowly and risk undermining the fundamental objectives of the AIE Directive)
.(emphasis added)”
43. The Court of Appeal in ESB gave its interpretation of Redmond at paragraph 87: “Redmond concerned a request for access to information regarding the sale of forestry land by Coillte Teoranta. In considering whether the information was environmental information, the Commissioner, and consequently the court, focused on whether the sale of land was a “measure affecting or likely to affect” the environment within the meaning of Article 3(1)(c). In that context Collins J. held that although a sale of land will not of itself result in any alteration to the land, it can nonetheless constitute a “measure” where there is evidence the purchaser intends to develop the land, even where such development would be subject to obtaining development consent. The test for whether the measure is likely to affect the environment is whether there is a real and substantial possibility it will affect the environment, whether directly or indirectly. A possibility must be more than remote or theoretical but need not amount to a probability that environmental impact will occur.”
44. It is clear that in order to determine whether the measure, is likely to affect the environment I must be persuaded there is a real and substantial possibility it will affect the environment, whether directly or indirectly. Accordingly, I have carefully considered the purpose of the Air Traffic Controllers investigation into the R116 air accident. In this regard, I have considered the detail AirNav have provided around such investigations generally. I have also considered the records it has provided me with in relation to this case specifically. These records include the IAA Safety Management Unit report into the R116 accident, and a partial transcript of Shannon Air Traffic Control to aircraft R116.
45. I consider that these records were utilised to establish the facts of what occurred in the lead up to the accident R116 air accident. I note that the AAIU as part of its investigation into the R116 air accident had access to both records, and aspects of these records were incorporated into the AAIU’s published final report. The purpose of the AAIU’s final report was to establish what happened, identify the causes and contributing factors and make safety recommendations to prevent similar air accidents in the future.
46. I have outlined the position of the parties in detail above. I have had regard to the decision and submission of AirNav Ireland, the information in the records subject to this appeal and the appellant’s submissions to this Office.
47. I note the appellant’s contention that the “real question is whether the content of the records fits within one or more of the categories in article 3(1), rather than how the records might be labelled in general terms”
and in her view that “the records clearly have the potential to fall within article 3(1)(c), which covers information on measures or activities affecting, or likely to affect, environmental elements”
.
48. As I have already set out, the test I need to be satisfied of is whether the Air Traffic Controllers investigation into the R116 air accident is a measure affecting or likely to affect the environment as it is the “measure”, not the information “on” that measure, that is subject to that threshold test (Redmond at paragraph 57). It is my view; there is no real and substantial possibility that the Air Traffic Controllers investigation into the R116 air accident, as a measure, is likely to affect the environment in the manner described in paragraph (c).
49. I consider that the connection between the measure, and any consequent effect on the environment to be overly remote and at best minimal and tenuous. It is important to reiterate, as it relates to the circumstances of this case, that there must be more than a minimal connection with the environment (Glawisching at paragraph 25) a mere connection of link to the environment is not sufficient to bring information within the definition of environmental information. Having carefully considered all submissions, I have not seen any evidence to persuade me of such a link.
50. I am not persuaded that the test as set out by the Court of Appeal in Redmond, that there is a real and substantial possibility that it will affect the environment, is met, even indirectly. The examples that the appellant has provided are, to my mind, too far removed to be considered anything more than a remote or theoretical possibility of effecting the environment. To find otherwise would plainly expand the scope of AIE in a manner that would be in direct contradiction to the judgments of the national courts and the CJEU, which have clearly determined that the scope of the definition of environmental information is broad but not unlimited, as referenced above.
Whether the information is on the measure or activity
51. Where the relevant measure or activity has the requisite environmental effect, one must consider whether the requested information is “on” that measure or activity within the meaning of article 3(1) of the AIE Regulations. In this case, having found that the relevant measure and/or activity i.e. the Air Traffic Controllers Report into the R116 air accident does not have the requisite environmental effect, it is not necessary for me to consider whether the requested information is “on” that measure or activity within the meaning of article 3(1) of the AIE Regulations.
52. I note the appellant in her submissions to this Office put forth several suggestions as to how the records - or relevant parts of them - fall within article 3(1)(a), (b), (c) and/or (f) (see paragraph 28). The final step to consider is whether the information requested by the appellant is information “on” the state of the elements of the environment and the factors likely to affect these elements.
53. The word “on” has been the subject of considerable litigation in the context of Article 3(1)(c). But there is nothing in those cases that limits their findings to the meaning of “on” in the context of paragraph (c) only and in my view the principles outlined in Henney are equally applicable to all of the paragraphs in the definition of environmental information.
54. The Court in Henney found that “information is ‘on’ a measure if it is about, relates to or concerns the measure in question (paragraph 37).” It is not sufficient for information to be merely connected to the measure or activity, but the information need not to be specifically, directly or immediately about the measure or activity.
55. In support of this conclusion, Henney further suggests that, in determining whether information is “on”
the relevant measure or activity, it may be relevant to consider the purpose of the information such as why it was produced, how important it is to that purpose, how it is to be used, and whether access to it advances the purposes of the Aarhus Convention and the AIE Directive (paragraph 43; see also ESB, paragraph 42). Information that does not advance the purposes of the Aarhus Convention and the AIE Directive may not be “on” the relevant measure or activity (Redmond, paragraph 99).
56. As the Court noted in Henney, the recitals of both the Aarhus Convention and the AIE Directive refer to the requirement that citizens have access to information to provide for a greater awareness of environmental matters, to enable more effective participation by the public in environmental decision-making and to facilitate the free exchange of views with the aim that all of this should lead, ultimately, to a better environment. Those recitals give an indication of how the very broad language of the text of the provisions in the Convention and Directive may have to be assessed and provide a framework for determining the question of whether information is on a particular measure. Finally, as the High Court noted in ESB information that is integral to a measure or activity is information “on” it while information that is too remote from the relevant measure or activity does not qualify as environmental information (ESB, paragraphs 38, 40, 41 and 43).
57. Taking in to account the specific facts and context of this appeal and having reviewed the records, I am of the view that the information is not environmental information as it is too remote without a real and substantial possibility that it will affect the elements and factors referred to in article 3(1)(a) and (b), directly or indirectly.
58. I have considered the examples provided by the appellant in support of her contention that the information could be capable of affecting the environment pursuant to article 3(1)(a) and (b). However, nothing in the appellant’s submissions or evident from the information before this Office has persuaded me that these suggestions amount to more than a theoretical link.
59. In light of the Courts commentary regarding the Aarhus Convention and the AIE Directive I have considered if citizens would be better informed and more able to contribute to environmental decision-making if they were able to access the information subject to this appeal. It is my view, that in the circumstances of this specific appeal, this would not be the case, and releasing the records would not serve to advance the aims of the Aarhus Convention and AIE Directive.
60. Accordingly, as I have found the definition of environmental information under article 3(1) has not been met, therefore an assessment of the exemptions applied by AirNav Ireland in support of its refusal of the appellant’s request i.e. articles 8(a)(iv) and 9(1)(b) of the AIE regulations, is not required in this instance.
61. Finally, the appellant in her appeal to this Office and in submissions dated 14 May 2026, refers to the final report into the R116 air accident having been completed and its findings published four years ago in November 2021. Also, the appellant refers to the “RTÉ’s Prime Time special on the Rescue 116 crash, which was broadcast on 05 November 2021, the night before the AAIU final report was published, and which the appellant contends “played actual transmissions between R116 and the Dublin Air Traffic Control.”
62. As I have determined that the information subject of the appeal is not considered to be environmental information in accordance with article 3(1) of the AIE Regulations, it is not necessary for me to comment on the above.
Decision
63. Having carried out a review under article 12(5) of the AIE Regulations, I affirm AirNav Ireland’s decision.
Appeal to the High Court
64. A party to the appeal or any other person affected by this decision may appeal to the High Court on a point of law from the decision. Such an appeal must be initiated not later than two months after notice of the decision was given to the person bringing the appeal.
Gemma Farrell
On behalf of the Commissioner for Environmental Information
